comments.author: Raju Dandigam
comments.comment:
Evals are usually the weakest layer because they get treated like a release gate instead of a production system.

The useful shift is logging failures as typed cases: retrieval miss, tool misuse, stale context, bad instruction following, unsafe action, or cost regression.

Without that taxonomy, teams keep tuning prompts when the real issue is often upstream.

comments.author: Neo Kim
comments.comment: I’d add failure-mode design to this list: timeouts, retries, fallbacks, tool-call validation, and human escalation paths. Most agent demos fail in production because the model is bad at one edge case, but because the system has no plan for partial failure.

comments.author: Dylan Anderson
comments.comment: The highest ROI boundary I’ve seen is forcing every agent step into one of three buckets: deterministic, model-mediated, or human-approved. If a step cannot explain why it needs a model, it probably should be code. If it can change money, permissions, customer state, or external systems, it probably needs a stop condition or approval gate.

comments.author: Jack Perschke
comments.comment: The best AI standards start with failure modes, not model choice. For RAG and agents, the real control points are retrieval quality, tool permissions, eval gates, audit logs, and a clear rollback path when the system is wrong.

comments.author: Stephen Olmstead
comments.comment: The hardest part of personal AI systems is not adding agents, it is reducing handoff cost. I’ve found the useful boundary is: one surface for thinking, one for delegated execution, and one for tiny disposable tasks. Anything beyond that needs a clear failure mode, or it becomes another dashboard to babysit.

comments.author: Yusen Tang
comments.comment: For noisy agent A/Bs, I’d start with paired evaluations: same initial states, same RNG seeds, swap player sides, then compare win-rate deltas with confidence intervals instead of raw aggregate wins. Elo or TrueSkill helps once you have many variants, but for architecture changes I’d still want a small fixed eval suite of “known hard states” so you can see whether the agent got better at decisions or just luckier over full episodes.
